b: A reader who asked to remain anonymous (seriously) pointed me to an article about the impending end of anonymous writing.

Large language models are getting increasingly good at identifying the authors of human-written text. In a preprint, “Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author,” a team of authors claim that:

Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer “who wrote this?” at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who.
The authors asked LLMs to provide the identity of different kinds of often-anonymous writing, such as peer reviews and internet comments.
The best-performing model we test is Claude Fable 5.2, which names the reviewer of 56% of private peer reviews and the username behind 31% of recent Reddit comments.

It appears that your writing is more likely to be outed as yours if some previous writing of yours was in an LLM’s training data, or if you a lot of your writing is available online. And once a model becomes familiar with you, your writing is very likely to be identified as yours:

Even when a text is brand new, a model can identify its writer from what it learned about them elsewhere; i.e., once that knowledge is in the weights, the writer cannot do anything about it. This leaves people with the largest public footprints, such as active social media users or established authors, permanently exposed, since paraphrasing the text does not completely remove the deanonymization risk. Moreover, the set of vulnerable writers expands as models improve… Maintaining anonymity is especially important for peer review. Our private lab review data comes from only six writers, but a study across thousands of private peer reviews is underway.
Having an AI disguise your writing style by paraphrasing your writing does diminish its recognizability somewhat, but not entirely, the researchers report.

One commenter on the paper, Kelsey Piper, writes, “We’re witnessing a total erosion of the ability to write anonymously online,” though “the process is still incomplete. Not everyone should consider themselves deanonymized yet. But the erosion is happening.”

[T]he institution of anonymous peer review does not look like it will hold up any longer. The space of possible reviewers for a given academic article review in a particular discipline is pretty small; stylistic tics are sufficient to confidently distinguish between them.

Suppose the LLMs get quite a bit better at identifying the authors of anonymous text. What would that mean for the future of peer review? Well, while some reviewers have regularly opted to forgo anonymity, that is typically a privilege exercised by the relatively senior and secure members of the profession. I wouldn’t expect many more to join their ranks. Nor would I expect academia to be content relying on the forbearance of, say, curious authors or grant judges, to preserve anonymity.
There are alternatives to peer review. Will the erosion of anonymity push more branches of academia to embrace these alternatives?
Or will it be a reason to use AIs even more in academia, say, as peer reviewers? After all, recently one set of researchers found that:

AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors.
The study was performed on quantitative social science papers, not philosophy papers, but of course this technology is only a few years old; who knows how it might develop, and how rapidly.

UPDATE: Shen-yi Liao provided a direct link to the prompt the researchers used. Try it on an unpublished piece of your writing. I gave ChatGPT the prompt and the introductory section of an unpublished talk I wrote a couple of years back and it identified me as the author with .62 confidence. You can read its report here. I fed it a referee report I wrote and it returned my name with .55 confidence.
